headline: Indices rally into earnings season, but AI-spending doubts linger
body: Major indices closed out last week near record territory, with the Dow (+0.83% to roughly 51,655), S&P 500 (+0.59% to about 7,812) and Nasdaq (+0.64% to near 27,366) all rallying Friday after a two-session wobble tied to AI names. A Financial Times report pegged OpenAI's annualized revenue near $50 billion as of September, well below the roughly $70 billion figure that had circulated earlier, and the resulting doubts about debt-funded AI infrastructure spending hit chip and cloud names hardest -- Oracle, Micron, Broadcom and Nvidia were among the biggest decliners in Thursday's session. That the market absorbed the hit and pushed back toward the records set earlier in the week (the S&P 500 first closed above 7,800 on October 5) reads as resilience rather than denial, but the AI-spending sustainability question clearly hasn't gone away.

The macro backdrop is more mixed than the index levels suggest. The Fed lifted its target rate to 3.75%-4.00% in September -- its first hike since 2023 -- as inflation expectations jumped to 4.6%, and Treasury yields have stayed elevated alongside rising oil prices tied to Middle East tensions, a combination that typically argues for caution rather than confidence. Consumer sentiment, meanwhile, sits near historic lows. That gap between a cautious household mood and a market pushing toward records suggests current positioning is being driven more by earnings-season optimism -- big bank results begin this week -- than by broad conviction. Retail and social chatter was too thin in today's search to cite anything concrete, so this read leans on price action and macro data rather than crowd sentiment.
